wip: Work in progress. This tab is a working prototype and is the only one on the page that is not translated — it stays in English in every language. Its ephemeris is validated (Sun and Moon to better than 35″ against libastro over 42 dates in 2026–27), but the interface, the viewpoint picker and the Moon's phase drawing are unfinished, and the flat model here covers azimuth only. Treat its numbers as sound and its edges as rough.
h1: Point a camera at a ridge at the right minute
lead: Every other tab on this page argues from measurements someone else published. This one hands you the instrument. Pick a date and a time, and it draws the Sun or the Moon at its true angular size against a skyline computed two ways from the same terrain — once on a plane, once on a sphere. The two curves separate by a measurable amount at certain azimuths. Go and photograph one of those azimuths at the stated minute, and the photograph decides.
sun-ruler: The Sun makes this cheap. Its disc is 32.4′ across, known to a fraction of an arcsecond, so a photograph containing both the disc and a ridge calibrates itself: the disc supplies the angular scale inside the frame. No theodolite, no known focal length, no assumption about where eye level was. And azimuth is immune to refraction, which is vertical — so the one prediction the flat map cannot rescue with weather is the one about direction.

Not ported yet: the baked DEM horizon silhouette, named viewpoints, the Moon's phase drawing and the map — the ridge is entered as distance and height, as the elevation-angle tab does.
